analysis.one_liner: Requires large employers to offer and help pay for workers' family health coverage.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing or a vote and died in committee with zero cosponsors when the 105th Congress ended in January 1999.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have amended the Fair Labor Standards Act to require employers with 50 or more workers to offer every employee a family health plan at least as generous as the Blue Cross/Blue Shield standard plan offered to federal workers, and to pay at least the same share of the premium the federal government pays for its own employees. It would have counted contract workers as employees, started coverage within 30 days of hire, and penalized employers who did not comply. It was referred to five committees and never moved.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers at companies with 50 or more employees who lack health coverage, and their spouses and children, would gain guaranteed access to a comprehensive employer plan with a defined employer contribution. Health insurers would also gain, since the bill forces employers to buy coverage from them.

how_it_helps.text: Would require every employer with 50 or more employees to offer each worker a family plan at least as generous as the Blue Cross/Blue Shield Standard Plan offered to federal employees, and to contribute at least the same share of the premium the federal government pays for its own workers.
Would treat contract workers as employees of the company they work for, closing a common gap in employer coverage.
Would require coverage to begin within 30 days of an employee's first hour of work, rather than after long waiting periods.
Would let states keep or add stricter coverage requirements on top of the federal floor, and back enforcement with civil money penalties and injunctions under the Fair Labor Standards Act.

analysis.who_pays: Large employers, who must pay a defined share of premiums and face civil money penalties if they do not comply. Employees pay their share of the premium through payroll withholding. Medicare and Medicaid would also be directed to pay the employee premium share for enrolled workers who take employer coverage.

drawbacks.text: The entire cost falls on employers with 50 or more workers, who must contribute to premiums for every employee including part-timers and contract workers; because employer mandates are a cost of hiring, some of that burden can come back to workers as slower wage growth or fewer jobs.
Covered employees must pay their share of the premium through payroll withholding, which reduces take-home pay even for low-wage workers.
The mandate covers only firms with 50 or more employees, so workers at small businesses — a large share of the uninsured — get nothing.

Workers on Medicare, Medicaid, FEHBP, or CHAMPUS would be required to accept employer coverage or have the federal program pay their premium share, shifting costs among public programs and steering people into private plans.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would have guaranteed affordable, comprehensive family coverage to millions of uninsured workers, funded by a defined employer contribution — a genuine benefit weighted toward ordinary working families. But it was an all-employer mandate with no subsidies: the full cost landed on large employers and employees' own paychecks, it left small-firm workers uncovered, and it reinforced employer-based private insurance rather than moving toward universal coverage. Even a supporter would concede the design was costly and incomplete.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in subcommittees of five different House committees from May 1998 until the Congress ended in January 1999, never getting a hearing, a markup, or a vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Frank Pallone introduced the bill on April 30, 1998, and no other member cosponsored it.

The Speaker referred it to five committees on the day of introduction — Education and the Workforce, Commerce, Ways and Means, Government Reform and Oversight, and National Security — splitting it across jurisdictions.

In May 1998 it was sent to subcommittees on Health and Environment, Health, Civil Service, Employer-Employee Relations, and Military Personnel; the only later action was a request for the Defense Department's comments on June 10, 1998.
No hearing, markup, or floor vote is recorded, and the 105th Congress ended on January 3, 1999 with the bill still in committee.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large employers came out ahead, avoiding a new requirement to help pay for their workers' health coverage. The uninsured workers the bill targeted gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Large employers avoiding a coverage mandate

for.name: Rep. Frank Pallone
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and argued in its findings that jobs should carry affordable family health coverage, as they do in every other industrialized country.

against.name: Chairs of the five committees of referral (Education and the Workforce, Commerce, Ways and Means, Government Reform and Oversight, National Security)
against.what_they_did: Received the referral, sent it to subcommittees, and took no further action; no hearing or markup was ever scheduled.

against.name: House cosponsors
against.what_they_did: No member of either party cosponsored the bill during its eight months in Congress.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken; the sponsor was a New Jersey Democrat and the bill attracted zero cosponsors from either party.

industries.note: The bill would have required them to contribute to family health premiums for every employee, including contract and most part-time workers, with civil money penalties for noncompliance. Their cost is precisely the coverage gain for workers.

A mandate on employers with 50 or more workers would create millions of new mandated customers, with plans required to match the federal employees' Blue Cross/Blue Shield standard. The bill channels coverage through private employer-based insurance rather than a public plan.
Because contract workers would count as employees, firms relying on contracted labor would have owed coverage contributions, reducing the advantage of using contractors instead of direct hires.
Exempt from the mandate, they would avoid the coverage cost their larger competitors must bear, though their own uncovered workers get no benefit.
